headline: Iran strikes US bases in Jordan and UAE
summary: Iran launched missiles and drones at US bases in Jordan and the UAE early on 31 August after a US strike on Larak Island, the first direct exchange since late July.
display_body: Iran fired missiles and drones at US bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates early on Monday 31 August, hours after a US strike on Iran's Larak Island — the first direct exchange between the two sides since late July and a sharp escalation in the six-month-old war. The United States said its forces hit two Iranian launchers on Larak Island, in the Strait of Hormuz (the narrow shipping chokepoint that carries roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil), on Sunday night 30 August. US Central Command (CENTCOM — the US military headquarters for the Middle East) characterised the operation as "limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat," and a US official told Al Jazeera the launchers were being readied to fire missiles carrying naval mines (underwater explosives that damage passing ships) toward the waterway. Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC, its elite military branch) said the US attack killed and wounded soldiers and civilians, and Tehran's foreign ministry called it "a direct violation of national sovereignty." In response, the IRGC said it struck the King Hussein and Al Azraq bases in Jordan and the Al Menhad airbase in the UAE, calling the Jordan strikes "a legitimate exercise of self-defence" under the UN Charter. Jordan's army said it intercepted eight Iranian missiles that breached its airspace at dawn; the UAE said its air force downed a drone approaching from Iran but rejected Iran's claim that its airbase was hit; and a US official said the attack on Jordan was intercepted. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran was "not looking for war" but would "give a decisive response to the aggressors." President Donald Trump separately claimed on Truth Social that Iran's Kharg Island — its main oil-export terminal — was being "blown to smithereens," a claim Iran has not confirmed and that no independent source has verified.
why: after weeks in which Washington had shifted from air strikes toward economic pressure (last week's sanctions package it branded "Operation Economic Outcast"), the tit-for-tat strikes are exactly the collapse of the diplomatic off-ramp that US and regional mediators had been trying to avoid — and they drag Jordan and the UAE directly into a war that has already disrupted Gulf oil shipping.

headline: SCO summit opens in Bishkek
summary: Xi, Putin, Modi and Iran's Pezeshkian gathered in Bishkek for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation's 25th-anniversary summit.
display_body: Leaders of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation opened a two-day summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Monday 31 August, with China's Xi Jinping, Russia's Vladimir Putin, India's Narendra Modi and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian all attending as the bloc marks its 25th anniversary. The SCO — a Eurasian security and economic grouping whose members account for about 43% of the world's population and roughly a quarter of global output — is meeting under the motto "Together for Sustainable Peace, Development and Prosperity," with Turkey's Erdogan and UN Secretary-General António Guterres also expected. On the agenda: the US-Israel war on Iran, the Russia-Ukraine war, and — pointedly — new trade and transport corridors that route around chokepoints, including the North-South corridor linking Russia to India through Iran and Arctic shipping via the Northern Sea Route, after the Strait of Hormuz disruption snarled global supply chains. A Modi-Putin bilateral is scheduled, and India-China border talks remain live after last year's rapprochement. Analysts cautioned the bloc is less a coherent anti-Western alliance than a venue where states hedge against US power.
why: the optics of Xi, Putin and Modi in one room, days after US strikes on Iran, are a deliberate signal of a "multipolar" alternative to Western institutions — though analysts expect rhetoric to outrun any concrete deals.

headline: Nepal flood toll passes 900
summary: The death toll from the Nepal-Tibet Himalayan glacial flood passed 900 with more than 4,000 still missing.
display_body: The death toll from the Nepal-Tibet Himalayan flash flood passed 900 by Monday 31 August, with more than 4,000 people still reported missing, as Nepal issued a fresh flood warning that briefly halted rescue work. The disaster began on Wednesday 26 August when a glacier collapse sent ice, rock and mud down the valleys of Nepal's Rasuwa district and across the Tibetan border, and the toll has climbed steeply — from about 470 confirmed dead on Thursday 28 August to over 900 now, on both sides of the frontier. The UN said the impact is "immense": aid teams are working around the clock to reach communities cut off in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading; the WHO has warned of disease risk from displacement and disrupted water and sanitation; and UNICEF says 18 schools were destroyed and about 10,000 children need support to keep studying. A "barrier lake" (a natural dam of landslide debris) and renewed flood alerts continue to threaten a second surge, and the UN's disaster-risk chief called it a "mountain hazard event" unseen "for a very, very long time."
why: it is among the deadliest glacial-outburst floods on record, and with thousands still missing and the danger not yet past, both the toll and the humanitarian need are still rising.

headline: Iceland rejects EU accession talks
summary: Icelandic voters rejected resuming EU accession talks 52.8% to 47.2% in a referendum.
display_body: Icelanders rejected resuming European Union accession talks, with the "No" camp winning 52.8% to 47.2%, according to the official count published by public broadcaster RÚV over the weekend of 30 August. Turnout was 82% of the roughly 270,000 eligible voters in the nation of about 400,000, and the capital Reykjavík was the only area to back membership. Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir, who had campaigned for "Yes," called the result "a victory for democracy" rather than a setback and confirmed her government will not pursue accession "this term," instead deepening ties through the European Economic Area (the arrangement that already gives Iceland access to the EU single market without full membership — the same framework Switzerland has repeatedly debated). European Council President António Costa said the bloc "fully respects the democratic choice" and called Iceland "one of the EU's closest and most trusted partners." Iceland first applied in 2009 after the financial crisis and suspended talks in 2013; the left-leaning government elected in 2024 brought the referendum forward amid rising tension over Russia's war and US interest in Greenland, with fishing rights and sovereignty the decisive concerns.
why: it settles, at least for this parliament, a question Iceland has wrestled with for over a decade — and it is a data point Swiss readers will recognise, another small European state opting to keep the EU at arm's length via the EEA rather than join.

headline: Gunman kills woman at Aarau rave
summary: A gunman killed an Italian woman and wounded five people at the Aarauer Rave on 30 August, triggering an international manhunt.
display_body: A gunman opened fire on the crowd at the annual Aarauer Rave in the early hours of Sunday 30 August, killing a young Italian woman and wounding five other people aged 24 to 27, some seriously, and triggering a national and international manhunt. The shooting happened before 3 a.m. at the Schachen racecourse in Aarau (a town of about 22,300, some 40 km west of Zürich) where the techno party was being held; the attacker or attackers fled and police say they cannot yet confirm whether it was one person or several, or how they escaped. Aargau cantonal police, backed by the federal police office Fedpol, have opened the search through Europol and Interpol and sent liaison officers to Aarau; police in Freiburg, across the German border, are also assisting, and investigators have appealed for phone videos from the event. Italy's foreign ministry confirmed the dead woman was an Italian national and said it is following the Swiss investigation closely.
why: a fatal mass shooting at a public event is rare in Switzerland despite widespread gun ownership, and the cross-border manhunt underscores how quickly a cantonal crime became a European police operation.

headline: Swiss gender pay gap narrows again
summary: Swiss federal data show the overall gender pay gap fell to 15.7% in 2024, with an unexplained gap of 6.5% or 640 francs a month.
display_body: Switzerland's gender pay gap narrowed again in 2024, with women earning on average 15.7% less than men, down from 16.2% in 2022, the Federal Statistical Office (BFS) reported on Monday 31 August. The figure continues a long decline (18% in 2020, 19% in 2018) and is based on standardised gross monthly wages converted to full-time. Part of the gap reflects structural factors — education, seniority, management roles, sector — but comparing women and men with the same profile still leaves an "unexplained" gap of 6.5% across the whole economy, or about 640 francs gross per month, down from 7.0% (657 francs) in 2022. The unexplained gap varies widely: about 31% in banking and insurance versus roughly 8% in hospitality, and it is larger in small firms (8.6% under 20 employees), in senior management (12.4%), and for older and married women. The BFS notes that traits like marital status can describe wage differences but do not justify them.
why: the unexplained portion is the part that legal equal-pay obligations target, so its slow-but-steady shrinkage — and where it stays stubbornly high — is the concrete measure of whether Swiss equal-pay policy is working.

headline: Bund taps feed reserves in drought
summary: Switzerland released compulsory animal-feed reserves as a record heat and drought summer strains farms.
display_body: The federal government has released compulsory feed reserves to help livestock farmers, as a record-breaking heat and drought summer leaves pastures parched across Switzerland. The opening of the national stockpile (Pflichtlager) for animal feed is the latest sign of strain from a summer SRF and the weather service describe as record-breaking: reservoir levels are running below average, several cantons and cities have only just lifted or loosened forest fire bans, and some farmers have resorted to importing hay from as far as Canada to keep herds fed. Foresters warn that even healthy-looking trees risk sudden branch failure after the prolonged dryness.
why: tapping strategic reserves normally held for emergencies is a tangible measure of how far this summer's drought has pushed Swiss agriculture, and it points to higher feed costs and pressure on domestic food production heading into autumn.
